title: Inversion for Emphasis — The Basics
subtitle: Flip the subject and auxiliary after a negative adverb, for dramatic emphasis.
objectives: Invert the subject and auxiliary after Never/Rarely/Seldom
Recognize this as a formal, written/spoken-for-effect structure, not everyday conversation

content.intro: When a negative or limiting word moves to the front of a sentence for emphasis, the subject and auxiliary swap places — just like in a question. This is the foundation; C1 will add more triggers and more nuance.

rules.heading: a) Never / Rarely / Seldom
rules.body:
Negative adverb + auxiliary + subject + main verb.

  • I have never seen such chaos. → Never have I seen such chaos.
  • She rarely complains. → Rarely does she complain.

rules.heading: b) Only after / Only when
rules.body: • She explained her decision only after the meeting. → Only after the meeting did she explain her decision.

rules.heading: c) Adding "do/does/did" when there's no auxiliary
rules.body:
If the original sentence has no auxiliary (simple present/past), add do/does/did before the subject.

  • She rarely complains. → Rarely does she complain.

examples: Never have I seen such chaos.
Only after the meeting did she explain her decision.
Never had he felt so proud.
Seldom do we get a chance like this.
Only when I saw the photo did I believe him.

commonMistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such chaos.
commonMistakes.right: Never have I seen such chaos.
commonMistakes.why: After the negative adverb, the auxiliary comes before the subject, like in a question.
With no auxiliary in the original sentence, you must add do/does/did.

commonMistakes.wrong: Only after the meeting she explained her decision.
commonMistakes.right: Only after the meeting did she explain her decision.
commonMistakes.why: "Only after..." also triggers inversion — add "did" and invert the subject.

items.prompt: Never ___ I ___ (see) such a beautiful sunset.

items.explanation: No auxiliary in the original — add "does" for the inversion.
"Only after" triggers inversion — add "did" for the past simple.
No auxiliary in the base sentence — add "do" and invert.

items.incorrect: Never I have felt so proud.
answer: Never have I felt so proud.
items.explanation: The auxiliary comes before the subject.

answer: Rarely does he call his parents.
items.explanation: Add "does" since there's no auxiliary in the original sentence.

summary: Only after/only when also trigger this inversion.
Add do/does/did when the original sentence has no auxiliary of its own.
This is formal/dramatic style — not used in everyday casual conversation.
